items.originalTitle: Google is making private AI practical with homomorphic encryption
items.summary:
Google has introduced HEIR, a new open-source compiler designed to enable cryptographically secure private AI inference using homomorphic encryption. This technology allows computations on encrypted data, preserving user privacy while enabling AI services without exposing sensitive information. HEIR aims to simplify the integration of encrypted inference into production applications by converting pre-trained AI models to operate on encrypted inputs.

HEIR is part of Google's broader private computing toolkit and addresses challenges in sectors like healthcare and finance, where data privacy is critical. The project has partnered with hardware accelerator companies and academic institutions to improve performance and foster research. Demonstrations include private content recommendations, credit card fraud detection, encrypted network traffic anomaly detection, and hotword detection, showcasing the practical applications of homomorphic encryption in AI.

items.originalTitle: Talos AI Agent Super Secure
items.summary:
Talos has developed an autonomous AI agent that runs on a user's own machine, taking instructions via chat and executing commands only after a deterministic security kernel authorizes each action. This design ensures that the language model proposes actions but never decides or executes them without explicit, time-limited tokens, enhancing security against unauthorized effects.

The agent operates under sandbox environments on Linux and macOS and refuses to run unprotected on unsupported platforms. It avoids multi-tenant use, external gateways, and web portals to minimize attack surfaces. Talos defends against mistaken or prompt-injected commands rather than malicious models and supports limited inbound communication methods without exposing the machine to public network access. The system maintains detailed audit trails and enforces strict authorization for every effect, aiming to provide a secure and testable autonomous agent framework.

items.title: Connecticut judge sanctions man for hiding AI prompt injections in court filings to sway case outcome [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Suspecting court of using AI, man injected prompts in filings to try to win case
items.summary:
A Connecticut judge identified a plaintiff who embedded hidden AI-readable prompts in court filings to influence the case in his favor, marking a likely first in the US legal system. The judge ruled the hidden text had no effect on the case outcome but called the tactic a dangerous precedent as AI use in courts grows.

The plaintiff, Matthew Elliott, used tiny white text invisible to humans but readable by AI systems to instruct any AI reviewing the filings to support his arguments and ignore prior court decisions. Despite warnings, Elliott continued adding hidden messages, including jokes and unrelated content, leading to sanctions for serious litigation abuse. The judge noted that Connecticut courts do not currently use AI to review filings, so the prompts posed no real risk but warned of future misuse as AI adoption increases.

The judge emphasized that if Elliott had concerns about AI use in the court, he should have raised them openly rather than covertly embedding commands. Elliott claimed his intent was to audit the court, but the judge found this explanation unconvincing. To prevent further abuse, the court barred Elliott from e-filing, requiring paper submissions instead, while acknowledging his pro se status and avoiding monetary penalties.

items.originalTitle: Vesta, adaptive ontology for Claude Code
items.summary:
Vesta is a companion tool that constructs and maintains a graph of a code repository, tracking references and definitions to help agents understand code structure without redundant processing. It operates locally without network calls, supports multiple languages via language servers, and provides commands to query repository composition, changes, defects, and rules enforcement.

The tool runs inference on the user's machine, storing derived data locally and excluding hidden or dependency directories from analysis. Vesta aims to improve code understanding by surfacing issues and vocabulary mappings during development, though its impact on productivity and defect detection has not yet been measured. It is available under the Apache 2.0 license and requires Python 3.10 or newer.

items.title: Anthropic launches watermark detection API for third parties to identify AI-generated text from Claude, based on Google's SynthID method [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Anthropic announces watermark detection API that will let third parties detect Claude's AI texts
items.summary:
Anthropic announced a new watermark detection API that allows third-party developers to verify whether text was generated by its Claude AI model. The watermarking technique modifies the randomness in word selection to embed a traceable pattern without affecting text quality, though it is less effective on short, fact-heavy, or heavily rewritten texts.

The feature is part of Anthropic's compliance with the EU AI Act and the EU Code of Practice on AI transparency, with watermarking enabled by default on all models released after August 2, 2025, and planned for older models soon. Unlike external AI detection tools that analyze text patterns, Anthropic's watermarking provides a more direct and reliable method to flag Claude's involvement in text creation, though it cannot confirm full authorship or distinguish from other AI models.

items.originalTitle: Taiwan targeted in AI-driven hacking campaign
items.summary:
Taiwan's Ministry of Digital Affairs reported that overseas hackers used AI agents to launch a cyberattack on government agencies last month, with the National Institute for Cyber Security issuing alerts starting July 20. The attack compromised at least 85 government user accounts and extracted more than 2,500 personnel records before expanding to Taiwan's nuclear safety agency and several energy companies.

The cyberattack was detected by Israeli AI start-up Dream, which identified the use of open-source AI agents to build an autonomous hacking tool. Communications linked to the operation were in simplified Chinese, suggesting a likely connection to China. The Ministry of Digital Affairs said the attack combined conventional hacking with AI agents like OpenClaw, enabling faster and more scalable attacks. Taiwan has since established guidelines to address AI-related cybersecurity threats and continues to strengthen its defenses.

items.title: Anthropic’s ‘First Lady’ Took a Winding Road to the Top
items.originalTitle: Anthropic’s ‘First Lady’ Took a Winding Road to the Top
items.summary:
Eric Schmidt had plenty of reasons to toast the success of Dario Amodei and Anthropic at a private event the former Google CEO hosted recently. But Schmidt, who is also an early Anthropic investor, made a point to celebrate “Cami and Dario,” the couple seated together at the event.

The Cami in question was Amodei’s wife, Camilla Clark, who has become a key behind-the-scenes player at Anthropic as the company has shot to prominence over the past year. As Amodei has hopscotched the globe to preach about the potential and risks of AI—from New Delhi to Davos to Sun Valley—Clark has almost always been near his side. Several people who know the couple describe Clark as Amodei’s emotional ballast, someone he has sought counsel from during the turbulence of Anthropic’s growth and clashes with Washington over the future of AI.

Clark may well be the most consequential person within Anthropic’s orbit who doesn’t have a formal role at the startup. You might even call her the first lady of Anthropic.
